en: O Mother, because you are naturally inclined toward speech, I worship you who are called Acyutā (the Imperishable).
You take away the multitude of my sins; yet, O Mother, by the power of my desire for you, I have instead gained the reputation of being "Aghahṛt" (the Remover of Sins).
Tell me, what connection could there possibly be between you and my words of wretchedness?

"That the son of Sāndīpani, who had long since entered the abode of Time, was brought back again into the presence of his parents—how is this the fame of Kṛṣṇa! Alas, if that son of the sage were not to worship Him with his tongue under the name of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, he would surely deserve a beating. (2)
That Hari’s act of theft and likewise his conduct as a paramour—
all this, through the power of narration, serves to destroy every sin;
thus has this majesty of yours, O Slayer of Madhu, been illuminated.
The playful charm of you, who wander here in the place called Kṛṣṇa while speaking thus, [is revealed]. || 3 ||
In the assembly hall, O Mother, when Draupadī’s slender garment was being pulled away by those seizing her clothes, her tongue—held back out of fear for her sari—rendered it thin and exposed;
yet you spread forth a mass of garments as vast as a mountain. Tell me, Govinda, from where did you obtain such a heap of cloth?
O Mother Acyutā,
the great ones declare you— who bear upon your tongue the forms of the lotus-born Brahmā and the other gods— to be worthy of worship;
yet that very tongue bows down even before horses, cattle, dogs, and the like.
Indeed, the path of your devotees is truly manifold.
O Mother, you who are named Murabhidā, you alone have arisen from the lotus-feet of the Discus-wielder as the river Jāhnavī for those who take refuge in him;
whereas for all others, the moon of his feet merely ripens [into mere water].
Indeed, in this world, there are rivers such as the Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, and others.
Not seeing Vainateya nearby, the Lord,
who had forcibly shaken off the lotus from his hand, was quickly brought by you to the one named Acyuta in order to subdue the king of elephants.
Speak, O Mother; without you, by whom was what experienced then?
Since I praise you, O protectress of the feet of the Three Ages, what loss could there be to your greatness? Indeed, my accomplishment is boundless;
for by even a dog, the divine river of the gods becomes an object of playful desire.
Then, what has become of her? She is suddenly overwhelmed by a weight of anguish. || 8 ||
Thus ends the Acyutāṣṭaka, composed by the venerable Śrīdhara Veṅkaṭeśārya.
